Stochastic Nonconvex Bilevel Optimization:
Improved Rates Without Rare-Visit Assumption

Daniel Cortild1 \orcidCortild    Mathias Staudigl2 \orcidStaudigl    Juan Peypouquet3 \orcidPeypouquet    Coralia Cartis1 \orcidCartis

1Mathematical Institute    University of Oxford    United Kingdom
2Department of Business Analytics and Decision Sciences   
University of Economics and Business    Vienna    Austria
3Bernouilli Institute    University of Groningen    The Netherlands
Last Compiled: September 6, 2026
Abstract

We investigate stochastic simple bilevel optimization with smooth and possibly nonconvex upper- and lower-level objectives. Existing stochastic extensions of dynamic barrier gradient descent (DBGD) either obtain fast convergence under an unverifiable trajectory-dependent “rare-visit” assumption, or remove this assumption at a substantially higher oracle cost. We show that a simple denominator-only regularization of the DBGD multiplier eliminates the need for such an assumption while preserving fast convergence rates. Specifically, our method achieves (ε,ε)(\varepsilon,\varepsilon)-stationarity in 𝒪⁡(ε−2)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) iterations using 𝒪⁡(ε−4)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4}) upper-level and 𝒪⁡(ε−7)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-7}) lower-level stochastic gradients, which improves upon the best assumption-free complexities. We additionally derive anytime parameter schedules.

Keywords. Simple Bilevel Programming, Stochastic Optimization, Dynamic Barrier.

1 Introduction

In this paper, we consider a simple stochastic nonconvex bilevel program, given by

minx∈˝{f(x):x∈\argminy∈˝g(y)},\min_{x\in\H{}}\left\{f(x)\colon\quad x\in\argmin_{y\in\H{}}g(y)\right\}, (P)

where f=\Exp​fξ,g=\Exp​gζ:→̋​\Rf=\Exp{f_{\xi}},g=\Exp{g_{\zeta}}\colon\H{\to}\R are defined over a real Hilbert space and are smooth and not necessarily convex, and only accessible through a stochastic oracle call. Here, the term simple refers to the fact that ff does not depend on the lower-level variable yy and gg does not depend on the upper-level variable xx. In this context, the lower-level function gg serves as a primary requirement, whereas the upper-level objective ff selects amongst lower-level solutions. This problem is also referred to as a nonconvex hierarchical program. Such a formulation has many applications, such as in hyperparameter training (Franceschi et al., 2018) or in machine unlearning (Reisizadeh et al., 2026), to name a few.

Even in a deterministic setting, nonconvex bilevel programs are hard. The lower-level constraint is global, and may have a nonconvex or even disconnected solution set. Therefore, classical ideas from convex bilevel programming, such as Tikhonov regularizations Kaushik and Yousefian (2021); Samadi and Yousefian (2025); Alves et al. (2025); Cortild et al. (2025b) or forming outer approxiations of the lower-level solution set Jiang et al. (2023); Cao et al. (2023); Cao et al. (2024) do not translate.

As solving Problem (P) to global optimality is intractable, we merely solve it to (εf,εg)(\varepsilon_{f},\varepsilon_{g})-stationarity, which was introduced in Cao et al. (2026) and will be rigorously defined in Section 2. It is such that ∇g​(x)\nabla g(x) is small, so that the point is nearly stationary for the lower-level, and such that there is no evident first-order direction that improves the upper-level objective.

To achieve this notion of stationarity, Cao et al. Cao et al. (2026) make use of Dynamic Barrier Gradient Descent (DBGD), originally proposed in Gong et al. (2021), which combines upper- and lower-level descent through an adaptive dual multiplier. Extending this approach to the present stochastic setting is nontrivial, as directly replacing the gradient by a stochastic estimator may cause singularities within the multiplier definition, since the lower-level gradient estimator may vanish away from stationary points.

Recently, Ahmadi et al. Ahmadi et al. (2026) address this issue by perturbing both the numerator and the denominator of the dual multiplier. The resulting method achieves fast rates under a trajectory-dependent “rare-visit” assumption, which is unverifiable a priori, and remove this condition through a penality-regularization, which leads to substantially slower rates. We instead perturb only the denominator, giving rise to

[β⁡(‖∇g‖2+ρ)−⟨∇f,∇g⟩]+‖∇g‖2+ρ⏟Ahmadi et al. Ahmadi et al. (2026)v.s.[β​‖∇g‖2−⟨∇f,∇g⟩]+‖∇g‖2+ρ⏟Ours.\underbrace{\frac{[\beta(\|\nabla g\|^{2}+\rho)-\langle\nabla f,\nabla g\rangle]_{+}}{\|\nabla g\|^{2}+\rho}}_{\text{Ahmadi et al. \cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{ahmadi_stochastic_2026}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}}}\quad\text{v.s.}\quad\underbrace{\frac{[\beta\|\nabla g\|^{2}-\langle\nabla f,\nabla g\rangle]_{+}}{\|\nabla g\|^{2}+\rho}}_{\text{Ours}}.

Despite the multipliers differing only by an additive constant in the numerator, this modification allows us to establish faster convergence rates under standard, verifiable assumptions. We provide a more thorough comparison of these works in Table 1.

Contributions. We propose a new algorithm, SDBGD, to solve Problem (P), converging to an (ε,ε)(\varepsilon,\varepsilon)-stationary point in 𝒪⁡(ε−2)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) iterations, requiring a total of 𝒪⁡(ε−4)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4}) stochastic oracle calls to ff and 𝒪⁡(ε−7)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-7}) stochastic oracle calls to gg. Importantly, we do not rely on an unverifiable assumption, such as the “rare-visit” assumption. We additionally provide anytime convergence rates, not requiring knowledge of the final horizon. We finally compare our method numerically to the ones proposed by Ahmadi et al. Ahmadi et al. (2026) on a simple example.

2 Problem Setup and Stationarity

Let be a real Hilbert space with associated inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle and induced norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|. We consider the stochastic simple bilevel problem

minx∈˝{f(x):x∈\argming},\min_{x\in\H{}}\left\{f(x)\colon\quad x\in\argmin g\right\}, (P)

where, for all x∈x\in, f⁡(x)=\ExpD​ξ​fξ​(x)f(x)=\ExpD{\xi}{f_{\xi}(x)} and g⁡(x)=\ExpD​ζ​gζ​(x)g(x)=\ExpD{\zeta}{g_{\zeta}(x)}, with fξ,gζ:→̋​\Rf_{\xi},g_{\zeta}\colon\H{\to}\R stochastic realizations of ff and gg respectively. We assume the following. {assumption} The expectations defining ff and gg are well-defined and differentiable, with, for all x∈x\in, ∇f(x)=\ExpDξ∇fξ(x)\nabla f(x)=\ExpD{\xi}{\nabla f_{\xi}(x)} and ∇g(x)=\ExpDζ∇gζ(x)\nabla g(x)=\ExpD{\zeta}{\nabla g_{\zeta}(x)}.

We further assume that \argmin​g≠∅\argmin g\neq\emptyset and that inff>−∞\inf f>-\infty.

We additionally assume the following.

{assumption}

There exist constants Lf,Lg,Gf>0,σf2,σg2≥0L_{f},L_{g},G_{f}>0,\sigma_{f}^{2},\sigma_{g}^{2}\geq 0 such that

  1. 1.

    ff and gg are respectively LfL_{f}- and LgL_{g}-smooth;

  2. 2.

    the upper-level gradient is uniformly bounded, namely ‖∇f​(x)‖≤Gf\|\nabla f(x)\|\leq G_{f} for all x∈x\in;

  3. 3.

    the stochastic gradients have uniformly bounded variance, namely

    \ExpD​ξ​‖∇fξ​(x)−∇f​(x)‖2≤σf2and\ExpD​ζ​‖∇gζ​(x)−∇g​(x)‖2≤σg2∀x∈.̋\ExpD{\xi}{\|\nabla f_{\xi}(x)-\nabla f(x)\|^{2}}\leq\sigma_{f}^{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\ExpD{\zeta}{\|\nabla g_{\zeta}(x)-\nabla g(x)\|^{2}}\leq\sigma_{g}^{2}\quad\forall x\in\H{.}

Uniformly bounded variance is a standard assumption in stochastic optimization Robbins and Siegmund (1971); Nemirovski et al. (2009), although recent trends aim to relax it under weaker growth or variance-at-solution conditions Bach and Moulines (2011); Needell et al. (2016); Khaled and Richtárik (2023); Alacaoglu et al. (2025); Cortild et al. (2025a); Garrigos et al. (2025); Cortild and Cartis (2026), at the cost of a more complex error handling. We retain the bounded-variance assumption here in order to simplify the results and isolate the difficulties arising from the stochasticity itself.

Assumption 2 does not require the lower-level gradient ∇g\nabla g to be uniformly bounded, nor does it require the individual realizations fξf_{\xi} and gζg_{\zeta} to be smooth. This is in contrast with Ahmadi et al. (2026), where boundedness of ∇g\nabla g is required, and smoothness of the stochastic realizations is used for their variance-reduced variant.

Since Problem (P) is nonconvex, we do not aim to solve it globally and instead introduce a notion of stationarity. We follow the convention of Cao et al. (2026) and measure stationarity in terms of squared gradient norms. This choice is equivalent to measuring it in terms of norms and rescaling (εf,εg)(\varepsilon_{f},\varepsilon_{g}), and is convenient as our analysis naturally controls the squared quantities.

Definition 2.1 ((εf,εg)(\varepsilon_{f},\varepsilon_{g})-stationarity Cao et al. (2026)).

A point x∈x\in is (εf,εg)(\varepsilon_{f},\varepsilon_{g})-stationary for Problem (P) if there exists λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 satisfying

∥∇f(x)+λ∇g(x)∥2≤εfand∥∇g(x)∥2≤εg.\|\nabla f(x)+\lambda\nabla g(x)\|^{2}\leq\varepsilon_{f}\quad\text{and}\quad\|\nabla g(x)\|^{2}\leq\varepsilon_{g}.

The second condition requires xx to be near-stationary for the lower-level objective. We emphasize that, since gg is nonconvex, lower-level stationarity does in general not mean proximity to \argmin​g\argmin g. Definition 2.1 should therefore be understood as a first-order approximation for solving Problem (P). The first condition describes first-order compatibility between the upper- and lower-level objectives. In fact, up to error εf\sqrt{\varepsilon_{f}}, the component of ∇f​(x)\nabla f(x) orthogonal to ∇g​(x)\nabla g(x) vanishes, while its parallel component either vanishes or points in the opposite direction to ∇g​(x)\nabla g(x). As such, there is no first-order direction that can substantially decrease ff without increasing gg.

3 Stochastic Dynamic Barrier Gradient Descent

The deterministic Dynamic Barrier Gradient Descent (DBGD) method of Cao et al. (2026) updates xkx_{k} with step-size ηk>0\eta_{k}>0 along the direction

dkDBGD=∇f(xk)+λkDBGD∇g(xk),λkDBGD=[βk​‖∇g​(xk)‖2−⟨∇f​(xk),∇g​(xk)⟩]+‖∇g​(xk)‖2.d_{k}^{\text{DBGD}}=\nabla f(x_{k})+\lambda_{k}^{\text{DBGD}}\nabla g(x_{k}),\quad\lambda_{k}^{\text{DBGD}}=\frac{[\beta_{k}\|\nabla g(x_{k})\|^{2}-\langle\nabla f(x_{k}),\nabla g(x_{k})\rangle]_{+}}{\|\nabla g(x_{k})\|^{2}}.

The choice of multiplier λkDBGD\lambda_{k}^{\text{DBGD}} is so that ⟨∇g​(xk),dkDBGD⟩≥βk​‖∇g​(xk)‖2\langle\nabla g(x_{k}),d_{k}^{\text{DBGD}}\rangle\geq\beta_{k}\|\nabla g(x_{k})\|^{2}, enforcing descent in the lower-level objective while retaining as much as possible in the upper-level. This multiplier may be viewed as the Lagrange multiplier associated with the projection problem min⁡{12​‖∇f​(xk)−d‖2:βk​‖∇g​(xk)‖2≤⟨d,∇g​(xk)⟩}\min\{\frac{1}{2}\|\nabla f(x_{k})-d\|^{2}\colon\;\beta_{k}\|\nabla g(x_{k})\|^{2}\leq\langle d,\nabla g(x_{k})\rangle\}, namely

λkDBGD=arg⁡maxλ≥0​mind​{12​‖∇f​(xk)−d‖2+λ⁡(βk​‖∇g​(xk)‖2−⟨d,∇g​(xk)⟩)}.\lambda_{k}^{\text{DBGD}}=\arg\max_{\lambda\geq 0}\min_{d}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\|\nabla f(x_{k})-d\|^{2}+\lambda(\beta_{k}\|\nabla g(x_{k})\|^{2}-\langle d,\nabla g(x_{k})\rangle)\right\}. (1)

The term dynamic barrier refers to the lower bound on ⟨d,∇g​(xk)⟩\langle d,\nabla g(x_{k})\rangle enforced in the projection dynamics, which provides a trade-off between loss minimization and constraint satisfaction, and is not directly related to an explicit barrier function.

In the stochastic setting, we no longer access the full gradients ∇g​(xk)\nabla g(x_{k}) and ∇f​(xk)\nabla f(x_{k}), but only unbiased stochastic mini-batch estimators of batch-sizes Bf,kB_{f,k} and Bg,kB_{g,k} respectively, given by

∇fk=1Bf,k​∑i=1Bf,k∇fξk,i​(xk)and∇gk=1Bg,k​∑j=1Bg,k∇gζk,j​(xk).\nabla f_{k}=\frac{1}{B_{f,k}}\sum_{i=1}^{B_{f,k}}\nabla f_{\xi_{k,i}}(x_{k})\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla g_{k}=\frac{1}{B_{g,k}}\sum_{j=1}^{B_{g,k}}\nabla g_{\zeta_{k,j}}(x_{k}). (2)

Directly substituting these quantities into the multiplier definition may be undefined, as ‖∇gk‖\|\nabla g_{k}\| may be small, or even zero, far from lower-level stationary points.

We instead regularize the denominator with a parameter ρk>0\rho_{k}>0, thus dividing by ‖∇gk‖2+ρk\|\nabla g_{k}\|^{2}+\rho_{k} rather than ‖∇gk‖2\|\nabla g_{k}\|^{2}. This prevents the singularity in the multiplier definition, while recovering the deterministic definition as ρk→0\rho_{k}\to 0. This yields the multiplier definition

λ^k=[βk​‖∇gk‖2−⟨∇fk,∇gk⟩]+‖∇gk‖2+ρk.\hat{\lambda}_{k}=\frac{[\beta_{k}\|\nabla g_{k}\|^{2}-\langle\nabla f_{k},\nabla g_{k}\rangle]_{+}}{\|\nabla g_{k}\|^{2}+\rho_{k}}. (3)

Importantly, unlike the multiplier definition in Ahmadi et al. (2026), we do not add a corresponding ρk​βk\rho_{k}\beta_{k} term to the numerator. Although the definitions are very similar, they lead to fundamentally different convergence properties, and require distinct arguments.

We introduce λk\lambda_{k} and dkd_{k} as quantities for our analysis, but they do not need to be computed:

λk=[βk​‖∇g​(xk)‖2−⟨∇f​(xk),∇g​(xk)⟩]+‖∇g​(xk)‖2+ρk,dk=∇f(xk)+λk∇g(xk).\lambda_{k}=\frac{[\beta_{k}\|\nabla g(x_{k})\|^{2}-\langle\nabla f(x_{k}),\nabla g(x_{k})\rangle]_{+}}{\|\nabla g(x_{k})\|^{2}+\rho_{k}},\quad d_{k}=\nabla f(x_{k})+\lambda_{k}\nabla g(x_{k}).

In the following algorithm, ηk>0\eta_{k}>0 is the step-size, βk>0\beta_{k}>0 is the barrier parameter, ρk>0\rho_{k}>0 is the regularization parameter, and Bf,k≥1B_{f,k}\geq 1 and Bg,k≥1B_{g,k}\geq 1 represent the batch-sizes for the upper- and lower-level gradient estimators, respectively.

{algorithm}

[H] Stochastic Dynamic Barrier Gradient Descent (SDBGD) {algorithmic} \Fork=0,…,K−1k=0,\ldots,K-1 \StateDraw independent ξk,i\xi_{k,i} and ζk,j\zeta_{k,j} for i=1,…,Bf,ki=1,\ldots,B_{f,k} and j=1,…,Bg,kj=1,\ldots,B_{g,k}. \StateDefine the independent mini-batches as in (2). \StateCompute λ^k\hat{\lambda}_{k} according to (3). \StateCompute d^k=∇fk+λ^k∇gk\hat{d}_{k}=\nabla f_{k}+\hat{\lambda}_{k}\nabla g_{k}. \StateUpdate xk+1=xk−ηk​d^kx_{k+1}=x_{k}-\eta_{k}\hat{d}_{k}. \EndFor

We make use of the random iterate xNKx_{N_{K}}, where NKN_{K} is drawn at random according to

ℙ⁡(NK=k)=ηk​βk∑k′=0K−1ηk′​βk′for k∈{0,…,K−1}.\mathbb{P}(N_{K}=k)=\frac{\eta_{k}\beta_{k}}{\sum_{k^{\prime}=0}^{K-1}\eta_{k^{\prime}}\beta_{k^{\prime}}}\quad\text{for $k\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\}$}. (4)

Balancing the stochastic error with the regularization parameter ρk\rho_{k} yields the following horizon-dependent and anytime rates. The proof is deferred to Appendix A.3, and all proportionality constants are independent of KK (or kk).

  1. 1.

    (Horizon-Dependent) Given a horizon K≥1K\geq 1, let a∈(0,1/3)a\in(0,1/3), and select

    ηk≡η∝K−a∈(0,(2​Lf+4​Lg)−1),βk≡β∝η−3​K−1∈(0,1),ρk≡ρ∝η−2​K−2,\eta_{k}\equiv\eta\propto K^{-a}\in(0,(2L_{f}+4L_{g})^{-1}),~~~\beta_{k}\equiv\beta\propto\eta^{-3}K^{-1}\in(0,1),~~~\rho_{k}\equiv\rho\propto\eta^{-2}K^{-2},

    Bf,k∝ηk4​(k+1)2,andBg,k∝max⁡(ηk−2,ηk6​(k+1)4).B_{f,k}\propto\eta_{k}^{4}(k+1)^{2},\quad\text{and}\quad B_{g,k}\propto\max(\eta_{k}^{-2},\eta_{k}^{6}(k+1)^{4}).

    Then it holds that, for any K≥2K\geq 2,

    \Exp​‖dNK‖2≤{dcases}​𝒪​(K−2​a)​if 0<a<1/4,𝒪⁡(K2​a−1​log⁡(K))​if 1/4≤a<1/3,\Exp{\|d_{N_{K}}\|^{2}}\leq\dcases\mathcal{O}(K^{-2a})\hskip 9.24994pt&\text{if $0<a<1/4$},\\ \mathcal{O}(K^{2a-1}\log(K))\text{if $1/4\leq a<1/3$},

    and

    \Exp​‖∇g​(xNK)‖2≤𝒪⁡(K−2​a​log⁡(K)).\Exp{\|\nabla g(x_{N_{K}})\|^{2}}\leq\mathcal{O}\left(K^{-2a}\log(K)\right).

The parameter a∈(0,1/3)a\in(0,1/3) controls the tradeoff between the two stationary residuals. The balanced choice a=1/4a=1/4 yields a rate of 𝒪(K−1/2){\mathcal{O}}(K^{-1/2}) or 𝒪~(K−1/2)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(K^{-1/2}) for both.

Corollary 3.2 (Oracle Complexity).

Under the horizon-dependent schedule of Corollary 3.1 with a=1/4a=1/4, we reach a (ε,ε)(\varepsilon,\varepsilon)-stationary point in 𝒪⁡(ε−2)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) iterations, resulting in 𝒪⁡(ε−4)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4}) upper-level and 𝒪⁡(ε−7)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-7}) lower-level stochastic oracle calls.

4 Numerical Illustration

We consider the following toy problem:

minx∈\R2{f(x)=1+‖x−c‖2:x∈\argminy=(y1,y2)∈\R2g(x)=2−cos(y1)−exp(−y22/2)},\min_{x\in\R^{2}}\left\{f(x)=\sqrt{1+\|x-c\|^{2}}\colon\quad x\in\argmin_{y=(y_{1},y_{2})\in\R^{2}}g(x)=2-\cos(y_{1})-\exp(-y_{2}^{2}/2)\right\},

using stochastic gradients ∇fξ=∇f+ξ\nabla f_{\xi}=\nabla f+\xi and ∇gζ=∇g+ζ\nabla g_{\zeta}=\nabla g+\zeta with Gaussian noise. We compare SDBGD with SDBPG, PR-SDBPG and VR-PR-SDBPG Ahmadi et al. (2026) under a common oracle budget of 10810^{8}, using anytime schedules for all methods. The details are provided in Appendix B.

In Figure 1, we plot the upper- and lower-level stationary measures for all four methods. While our method does not empirically improve upon the previously proposed ones, its theoretical guarantees are stronger and does not require any unverifiable assumption.

5 Conclusion

We introduced SDBGD, a denominator-regularized stochastic variant of DBGD Cao et al. (2026) for stochastic simple nonconvex bilevel programming. Under standard assumptions, SDBGD achieves 𝒪⁡(ε−2)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) iteration complexity, using 𝒪⁡(ε−4)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4}) upper-level and 𝒪⁡(ε−7)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-7}) lower-level stochastic oracle calls. These rates do not require an unverifiable trajectory-dependent “rare-visit” assumption as in Ahmadi et al. (2026), and improve upon the assumption-free guarantees of Ahmadi et al. (2026). We additionally provided an anytime parameter schedule and a simple numerical illustration. Overall, our results show that minor differences in the multiplier definition can substantially affect the theoretical guarantees.

Open Question. The stochastic variants of DBGD proposed here and in Ahmadi et al. (2026) differ only slightly in their multiplier definition, yet yield considerably different guarantees. This suggests directly substituting the gradient for a stochastic estimator thereof may not be the natural stochastic analogue of DBGD. Since deterministic DBGD admits a projected dynamical system interpretation (1), an interesting direction might be to consider a stochastic projected dynamical system to derive the stochastic multiplier. We leave the following for future work:

What is the appropriate stochastic analogue of deterministic multiplier-based bilevel methods?

Appendix B Experimental Setup

The goal of the numerical example in Section 4 is to provide a toy example showcasing a comparison between the methods SDBGD, SDBPG, PR-SDBPG and VR-PR-SDBPG. In this section, we provide a complete description of the experiment, allowing for complete reproducability.

Problem Setup. As mentioning in Section 4, we select

f(x)=1+‖x−c‖2andg(x1,x2)=2−cos(x1)−exp(−x22/2),f(x)=\sqrt{1+\|x-c\|^{2}}\quad\text{and}\quad g(x_{1},x_{2})=2-\cos(x_{1})-\exp(-x_{2}^{2}/2),

where c=(7.1,1)c=(7.1,1). This choices implies that

\argmin​g={(2​π​m,0):m∈ℤ},\argmin g=\{(2\pi m,0)\colon m\in\mathbb{Z}\},

so that the solution to (P) is (2​π,0)(2\pi,0). These functions satisfy our assumptions with Lf=1,Lg=1,Gf=1L_{f}=1,L_{g}=1,G_{f}=1.

Stochastic Oracle. We having access to stochastic gradients given by

∇fξ​(x)=∇f​(x)+ξand∇gζ​(x)=∇g​(x)+ζ,\nabla f_{\xi}(x)=\nabla f(x)+\xi\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla g_{\zeta}(x)=\nabla g(x)+\zeta,

where ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,σf2​I)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{f}^{2}I) and ζ∼𝒩⁡(0,σg2​I)\zeta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{g}^{2}I), so that assumption of uniformly bounded variance is satisfied. We select σf=σg=0.5\sigma_{f}=\sigma_{g}=0.5.

Algorithmic Setup. All methods are implemented in an anytimes fashion. Our method, SDBGD, uses the anytime schedule described in Corollary 3.1 with a=1/4a=1/4. For the methods in Ahmadi et al. [1], whose theory only cover horizon-dependent schedules, we form anytime schedules by replacing the horizon KK by the current effective horizon k+1k+1. Each method is started at the same initial point x0=(1.5,1.5)x_{0}=(1.5,1.5) and is given the same stochastic oracle budget ℬ=108\mathcal{B}=10^{8}.

Parameter Selection. The choice of parameters is given in Table 2. The powers of tk=(k+1)t_{k}=(k+1) follow the theoretical results, whereas the proportionality constants are chosen manually and not varied between runs.

Oracle Accounting. During iteration kk, the methods SDBGD, SDBPG and PR-SDBPG use Bf,k+Bg,kB_{f,k}+B_{g,k} stochastic oracle calls. Method VR-PR-SDBPG makes use of 2​(Bf,k+Bg,k)2(B_{f,k}+B_{g,k}). An iteration is executed only if its complete oracle cost fits within the remaining oracle budget.

Evaluation Protocol. We perform 1010 independent runs, and plot the empirical mean of the upper-level stationarity measure ‖dk‖2\|d_{k}\|^{2} and if the lower-level stationarity measure ‖∇g​(xk)‖2\|\nabla g(x_{k})\|^{2}. We note that full gradients are only used for evaluation purposes and are never called by the algorithm.

Computer Resources. The experiment is written in Python 3.13, and was executed on an Apple Silicon MacBook Pro, with a M5 chip and 16GB of RAM.

Code Availability. The code is available on the author’s GitHub page: https://github.com/DanielCortild/Stochastic-Nonconvex-Bilevel.
